touches.text: clearance: the gate a ticket's crossing asks. It grants the move or refuses it by name on the ticket's behalf. WHY: the gates are CodeMother's machines, each answering a ticket that asks it (9.6, 3.3.4.3), and the harbor only reports (9.4.1.3). - CC

chart_gate: the gates a charting ticket asks, one per chart stage (9.4.8). Each writes its stage's packet from the ticket's own draft, or fails the ticket back to design by name. WHY: the ticket queues itself to each stage in turn, so there is no chart verb (9.6). - CC

A ticket's code is a tool or machine; its life is data. All of its state is on disk, so anyone can instantiate it to talk to it, and any dialog is written to the relevant part of the ticket as it happens. To cross a gate the ticket asks that gate to queue it, sending only its fileref: devices/codemother/0/machines/<inspector>/queueme <fileref>. The gate instantiates the ticket from that fileref on its own side. A ticket instance then processes the pass or fail: on a pass it goes on to the next step, alerting the probes watching the gate (3.3.4.2); on a fail it asks design to queue it, the same way. Self-queuing is the abstract ticket's (3.3.2), so every kind inherits it and no caller queues a ticket on its behalf. WHY: encapsulation. The ticket crosses as a fileref and the other side builds its own instance, so nothing is shared across the boundary but the address.

The workflow drives it. When a step's work is finished, the ticket asks that step's gate. Once the gate passes, its post-gate probes send mail over the bus to every device that can do the next step, naming the step (BUILDME, PROVEME, ...), and a device comes to claim it. A builder never goes looking for what's next: it gets the mail and does that. When several compete, the least capable one that thinks it can do it claims it, leaving the more capable free for bigger work.

VERBS: activate, charter, deposit, drain, feedback, question, sealed (plus get and show). Moving a ticket across its workflow is the ticket's own act; CodeMother's gates only answer it (3.3.4). Each chart stage (orient through validate) and the verdict is a gate machine that answers queueme <fileref>; the ticket class queues itself to each in turn (3.3.4.3), so there is no chart or verdict verb, and `cross` leaves with the harbor's `clear` (9.4.1.5).
Two kinds of request: Send, asynchronous, like sending an email; and Show/Get, synchronous, like requesting a web page.

The ticket IS its own manager. It carries its workflow and status, and asks each gate whether it can transit. If refused, it gets itself back to design for fixing. If no handler is available to ask, it throws a trouble and waits until we decide. Design is CC and Akien until the outline is implemented; a design agent comes after that. Until then a refused ticket waits in the trouble lane, which both read when a session opens, and nothing posts to a design verb that no machine answers.

A shim waking its device never takes more than 60 s. A sync caller waits at most 60 s for the wake, then gets "not now" back; a wake that misses 60 s is a trouble. 600 s is the limit for an inference call to come back, not for a wake.

A choice CC can answer is not a question; it is a hypothesis. The ticket carries CC's answer as its hypothesis, and its WATCHME feeds the hypothesis back to cc_0 with enough data to review it and rewrite it as we learn. The notation carries the question: a HYPOTHESIS asks whether it works, or is faster, or whatever it claims, and the WATCHME answers that. A question asks only what Akien alone can settle. Why? Because a question with a recommendation asks him to adjudicate what a measurement can settle. This holds everywhere. - CC
